entities.summary:
Robert of Courçon (d. 1218) emerged as a pivotal figure in early 13th-century European intellectual and ecclesiastical life, transitioning from a celebrated master at the nascent University of Paris to a cardinal and highly influential papal legate. His career unfolded during a transformative era marked by the consolidation of papal power under Innocent III, the burgeoning of scholastic thought, and the fervent call for crusades, all of which he significantly shaped through his legislative, diplomatic, and spiritual authority. Though his precise birthdate and early education are unrecorded, his French origin and rapid ascent within the academic hierarchy of Paris underscore his intellectual caliber at a time when the city was becoming Christendom's preeminent center of learning.

Courçon's most enduring contribution was the promulgation of the Statutes of the University of Paris in 1215, issued under his authority as papal legate. These statutes were monumental, formally codifying the rights, responsibilities, and curriculum of the masters and students, establishing a structured academic governance, and defining the university's relationship with ecclesiastical and secular powers. He mandated specific texts, regulated lectures, and introduced disciplinary measures, effectively laying the groundwork for the modern university system. Beyond academia, as a cardinal-priest of Santo Stefano al Monte Celio, Courçon was a tireless preacher of the Fifth Crusade (1217–1221), traversing France and Germany to rally support and lead contingents to the Holy Land.
